title: Double herringbone stitch
subtitle: Two passes of herringbone interlaced to fill a band
excerpt: Double herringbone stitch lays a second row of herringbone over the first so that the two rows interlock at the crossings. The result is a dense, woven-looking band with a distinctive lattice surface.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), herringbone entry.

content.text: Double herringbone stitch is a two-pass stitch. The first pass lays an open herringbone band between two guide lines. The second pass works through the same band, threading under and over the first-pass crossings so that the two rows lock together without the needle entering the fabric on the second pass (except to secure at each end). Spacing must be even on the first pass or the second pass will not interlace neatly.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 2 to 3 strands; use a contrasting colour for the second pass to show the interlacing

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 9 for first pass; tapestry needle size 24 for second pass

content.text: Draw two parallel lines about 10 mm apart. Work a complete row of open herringbone stitch from left to right, keeping the forward step and the backward step even throughout. Leave a gap between each crossing so the second pass can travel through.
Secure the second thread and bring it up at A on the bottom guide line, just to the left of the first stitch. Travel to the right along the same band.

At each crossing of the first pass, slide the tapestry needle under the first-pass thread that is on top, then over the thread beneath it. Do not pierce the fabric. This locks the two layers together.

At the guide lines, take the needle into the fabric at B (top or bottom) as a normal herringbone stitch step, then bring it up for the next diagonal. Continue to the end of the band and secure on the back.
Check the surface: the two colours should alternate at each crossing along both guide lines, producing a woven lattice.

items.symptom: The second pass cannot thread through evenly
items.cause: First-pass stitches are spaced unevenly, so the gaps between crossings are inconsistent.
items.fix: Re-stitch the first pass with a ruler or marked dots at equal intervals before starting.

items.symptom: The lattice looks tangled rather than woven
items.cause: The second pass went under and under (or over and over) at the same crossing instead of alternating.
items.fix: Pull back to the last correct crossing and re-thread, checking you go under the top thread and over the lower thread at each point.
